content.overview: BNS s. 36 — Right of private defence against act of a person of unsound mind, etc.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Right of private defence against act of a person of unsound mind, etc. BNS restatement of IPC 98. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 98. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 36 is the rule on “Right of private defence against act of a person of unsound mind, etc”. The section provides that when an act, which would otherwise be a certain offence, is not that offence, by reason of the youth, the want of maturity of understanding, the unsoundness of mind or the intoxication of the person doing that act, or by reason of any misconception on the part of that person, every person has the same right of private defence against that act which he would have if the act were that offence. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 36 exists so that “Right of private defence against act of a person of unsound mind, etc” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
36. When an act, which would otherwise be a certain offence, is not that offence, by reason of the youth, the want of maturity of understanding, the unsoundness of mind or the intoxication of the person doing that act, or by reason of any misconception on the part of that person, every person has the same right of private defence against that act which he would have if the act were that offence

Essential ingredients
1. When an act, which would otherwise be a certain offence, is not that offence, by reason of the youth, the want of maturity of understanding, the unsoundness of mind or the intoxication of the person doing that act, or by reason of any misconception on the part of that person, every person has the same right of private defence against that act which he would have if the act were that offence

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). Z, a person of unsound mind, attempts to kill A; Z is guilty of no offence. But A has the same right of private defence which he would have if Z were sane

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 36 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Illustration (b). A enters by night a house which he is legally entitled to enter. Z, in good faith, taking A for a house-breaker, attacks A. Here Z, by attacking A under this misconception, commits no offence. But A has the same right of private defence against Z, which he would have if Z were not acting under that misconception

Exam use: quote illustration (b), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 36 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) When an act, which would otherwise be a certain offence, is not that offence, by reason of the youth, the want of maturity of understanding, the unsoundness of mind or the intoxication of the person doing that act, or by reason of any misconception on the part of that person, every person has the same right of private defence against that act which he would have if the act were that offence
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 36 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 36 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

learningObjectives: Understand the right of private defence against legally exempted attackers under BNS s. 36.
Analyze the principle that absence of mens rea in the attacker does not extinguish the defender's right.
Identify the five exempt categories: youth, unsoundness, intoxication, misconception, or want of understanding.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 36 provides that when an act, which would otherwise be a certain offence, is not that offence, by reason of the youth, the want of maturity of understanding, the unsoundness of mind, or the intoxication of the person doing it, or by reason of any misconception on the part of that person, every person has the same right of private defence against that act which he would have if the act were that offence.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The right of private defence is directed against the physical danger threatened by an act, not against the moral or legal culpability of the actor. The fact that the attacker is a lunatic, an infant, an intoxicated person, or mistaken does not deprive the victim of the right to defend his life and property.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 36 (corresponding to IPC s. 98).
Scope: Clarifies that attacker's personal immunity does NOT negate victim's right of defence.
Exempted conditions in attacker: (1) Youth (s. 20), (2) Immaturity of understanding (s. 21), (3) Unsoundness of mind (s. 22), (4) Intoxication (s. 23), (5) Misconception of fact (s. 14/17).
essentialIngredients: An act was committed which would be an offence but for the personal incapacity or exemption of the doer.
The incapacity arose from youth, immature understanding, insanity, intoxication, or mistake.
The victim exercised private defence as if the act were an offence.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: In criminal jurisprudence, an act committed by a lunatic (s. 22) or a child under seven (s. 20) is 'no offence'. If private defence only existed against 'offences', a victim attacked by an insane person with a sword would have no legal right to strike back. Section 36 removes this absurdity. It declares that the victim's right of self-preservation remains identical whether the attacker is fully sane or completely exempt from penal liability. The law protects the body and property from physical harm regardless of the attacker's criminal capacity.
examples: Teaching example (Lunatic attack): Z, under the influence of severe delusions, attempts to kill A with a meat cleaver. Z is guilty of no offence under s. 22. A has the same right of private defence against Z which he would have if Z were sane; A may strike Z to save his life.

Teaching example (Night traveler misconception): A enters by night into a house which he is legally entitled to enter. Z, in good faith mistaking A for a housebreaker, attacks A. A has the same right of private defence against Z which he would have if Z were not acting under a misconception of fact.
distinctions: Moral guilt of attacker vs Victim's right to life: Attacker's personal defence under ss. 20–23 does not diminish victim's defensive rights under s. 36.
Mutual private defence under mistake: In exceptional situations of mutual factual misconception, both parties may simultaneously have rights of private defence under s. 36.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an individual who used force to disarm an eight-year-old child firing a real revolver can claim private defence under BNS s. 36.
Rule: Section 36 preserves the right of private defence against acts committed by children lacking maturity.
Application: The child's personal immunity under s. 20/21 does not strip the defender of the right to preserve his life.
Conclusion: Section 36 applies; the defensive act is lawful.
